title: The Scientific Revolution
summary: From 1543, when Copernicus's sun-centred astronomy and Vesalius's anatomy were printed, to Newton's Principia of 1687, European natural philosophers remade astronomy, anatomy and mechanics. Historians still dispute whether it was one revolution and how much it owed to Islamic astronomy.
card: Between the printing of Copernicus's De revolutionibus and Vesalius's Fabrica in 1543 and the publication of Newton's Principia in 1687, astronomers, anatomists and natural philosophers in Europe replaced the inherited Aristotelian-Ptolemaic-Galenic picture with sun-centred astronomy, elliptical orbits, telescopic evidence and a single mathematical law of motion and gravity. New institutions such as the Royal Society, founded in London in 1660, gave the work a shared forum. Historians now argue over whether this was a single coherent revolution at all, and scholars such as Jamil Ragep argue that Copernicus built on Islamic astronomers.
what:
The Scientific Revolution is the name historians give to a run of changes in European understanding of the heavens, the human body and motion, usually dated from 1543 to 1687. In 1543 two books were printed within months of each other: Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium at Nuremberg, which set out a mathematical model with the Sun near the centre, and Andreas Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica at Basel, a seven-book anatomy that corrected Galen from dissection. Tycho Brahe's long series of planetary observations let Johannes Kepler show, in his Astronomia nova of 1609, that Mars moves in an ellipse and sweeps equal areas in equal times; he added a third law in 1619. In March 1610 Galileo Galilei announced four moons of Jupiter seen through a telescope, evidence against the idea that everything circles the Earth. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition convicted him of vehement suspicion of heresy for defending the Copernican view, and he lived under house arrest. In 1660 a group meeting at Gresham College, London, began the body that received a royal charter in 1662 as the Royal Society, which from 1665 issued the Philosophical Transactions. In 1687 Isaac Newton published the Principia, deriving Kepler's laws from three laws of motion and a universal inverse-square gravitation.

Whether this was one revolution is disputed. Herbert Butterfield's 1949 account treated it as the founding moment of modern science, while Steven Shapin opened a 1996 book by denying that any such single event occurred, and continuity historians stress the medieval roots of the figures involved. The usual end date is Newton, but other bounds have been proposed. Another dispute concerns Islamic astronomy: Jamil Ragep argues that devices from the thirteenth-century Maragha school and from Ibn al-Shatir reached Copernicus, while sceptics hold that he may have reinvented them.

uncertainty.note: The bounds are a convention, not an observed boundary. 1543 is the year De revolutionibus and the Fabrica were printed; 1687 is the first edition of the Principia. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes the period as roughly 150 years from Copernicus to Newton and notes that historians propose other starts and ends, so earlier roots (the Islamic astronomy of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries) and later extensions are not included.

how: Several lines converged rather than one cause. Printing let diagrams and tables be reproduced identically: De revolutionibus came from the Nuremberg press of Johannes Petreius, and the Fabrica's woodcuts were sent over the Alps from Venice to Basel for Johannes Oporinus. Copernicus accepted Ptolemy's data but wanted uniform circular motion, and reached a Sun-centred arrangement; his book was often read as a better calculating device rather than a physical claim, helped by Osiander's preface. Kepler used Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars to replace circles with ellipses (1609). Galileo's telescope, from 1610, produced new evidence such as Jupiter's moons. Newton's Principia (1687) showed that an inverse-square central force gives Kepler's laws, tying the heavens to terrestrial mechanics. In the background, a Muslim-world tradition of astronomy, including the Tusi couple (13 February 1247) and Ibn al-Shatir's models, supplied mathematical tools, and the Royal Society, with its 1662 charter and 1665 Philosophical Transactions, offered a way to circulate and check claims.
why_it_matters: The immediate consequence was a new picture of the cosmos and a new way of settling disputes about it. After Newton, a single mathematical law accounted for falling bodies, the Moon and the planets, so that heavens and Earth were no longer governed by separate physics. Habits that the period made routine, including publishing results in an accountable journal such as the Philosophical Transactions, and relying on instruments and repeatable trials instead of ancient authority, still organise research. Vesalius's book showed that Galen could be corrected from the body itself, though critics such as his former teacher Jacques Dubois resisted. The period also had costs and limits: the Inquisition convicted Galileo in 1633, and Copernicus's book stayed on the Index of Prohibited Books from 1616 to 1758, after being corrected rather than banned outright. The debate over its origins matters too. If Ragep is right that Copernicus drew on Maragha and Ibn al-Shatir, then the story of a purely European breakthrough is incomplete; if the sceptics are right, similar problems led independent astronomers to similar solutions. Without the 1543 books, the 1609 laws, the telescope and the Principia arriving in this sequence, later work on engines, navigation and engineering would have lacked a shared mathematical mechanics, and the Industrial Revolution would likely have looked different.

perspectives.holder: Founding-revolution view (Herbert Butterfield 1949; A. Rupert Hall; David Wootton 2015)
perspectives.account: The period from Copernicus to Newton produced a decisive break and a new kind of knowledge, a watershed in which modern science was founded.

perspectives.holder: Continuity and sceptical view (Pierre Duhem, A. C. Crombie, John Herman Randall; Steven Shapin 1996)
perspectives.account: Figures usually called revolutionaries worked inside medieval and Renaissance traditions, and Shapin opens a 1996 book by denying that a single event called the Scientific Revolution occurred.

Cohen proposed tests for attributing a revolution (contemporary perception, documents, later historians, later scientists); Kuhn later gave up Butterfield's idea of founding revolutions; Bowler and Morus question whether most developments fit Kuhn's standard.

Devices such as the Tusi couple and Ibn al-Shatir's models appear in De revolutionibus, as does Ali Qushji's physics of a rotating Earth, and intercultural transmission is a more compelling explanation than parallel discovery.

perspectives.holder: Mario di Bono (as described by Ragep 2014); Andre Goddu
perspectives.account: Copernicus, facing the same problems in Ptolemy's models, may have independently reached the same devices, and the transmission is not proved; Ragep notes that none of the European actors left any hint of independent invention.
